strengths: The core theoretical contribution is clean and well-executed: the paper derives, via a standard bias-variance decomposition, a closed-form optimal shrinkage coefficient (Theorem 1) that combines per-prompt and cross-prompt (batch) mean-reward estimates, and proves (Proposition 1) that a carefully constructed leave-one-out version of the estimator preserves unbiasedness of the policy gradient -- a nontrivial and important requirement that the naive shrinkage baseline (Eq. 9) does not satisfy.

The proposed baseline is a genuine drop-in replacement: it introduces no new hyperparameters, requires negligible extra computation (few lines of code, shown in Appendix D.1), and unifies/generalizes existing baselines (RLOO/per-prompt mean and REINFORCE++/batch mean) as special cases in limiting regimes of v2 and s2, giving good interpretability.

Empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this kind of methods paper: math reasoning (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B, Qwen3-4B-Base on DAPO17k), logic puzzles (Knights-and-Knaves, Countdown, Maze across multiple model families/sizes), multimodal reasoning (Geometry3k with Qwen2.5-VL), and RLHF with a Bradley-Terry reward model (Llama-3.2-3B) -- consistent gains are shown across all settings.

The paper goes beyond downstream accuracy and directly verifies the theoretical variance-reduction claim: Appendix B estimates ground-truth value functions and policy gradients via large-scale Monte Carlo sampling and shows the shrinkage baseline yields lower MSE against the true value function and lower L2 error against the true policy gradient, which is convincing direct evidence rather than only indirect (accuracy-based) evidence.

Useful ablations on dataset difficulty heterogeneity and semantic heterogeneity (Appendix C) probe when/why the adaptive shrinkage coefficient helps, and the analysis of training dynamics (adaptive decay of the shrinkage coefficient with more rollouts and over training) adds interpretability and supports the theoretical predictions.

Reproducibility support is reasonably strong: explicit code listing for the estimator, explicit unbiased gradient-variance estimator derivation and pseudocode, and comprehensive hyperparameter tables for every experiment in the appendix.
weaknesses: The connection to the classical James-Stein/Stein's paradox result is somewhat oversold as branding: the actual derivation is a scalar bias-variance-optimal convex combination of two unbiased estimators (essentially inverse-variance weighting/empirical-Bayes shrinkage), which is a well-known and comparatively simple statistical result, not the full multivariate James-Stein estimator (which relies on dimension >= 3 and a specific shrinkage factor involving ||X-mu||^2). The paper's own admission that 'the classical James-Stein guarantees do not directly apply' underscores that the theoretical novelty for the statistics community is modest; the contribution is primarily its careful, unbiased adaptation to the RLVR batch/rollout structure.

The reduction from 'minimize policy-gradient variance (trace of covariance)' to 'minimize baseline MSE w.r.t. the value function' (Section 3.1, Eq. 3-4) relies on an admittedly heuristic simplification that ignores the score-function norm weighting; this is standard in the literature but means the paper's claim of 'provable variance reduction' for the actual policy-gradient estimator (not just the baseline MSE) is only approximate/heuristic rather than fully rigorous, which slightly overstates the strength of the theoretical guarantee in the abstract/intro.

The optimal shrinkage coefficient depends on plug-in estimates of v2 and s2 (Eqs. 13-15) computed from the same small batch (e.g., only 2-8 rollouts per prompt in several experiments); there is no analysis of the estimation error/variance of the shrinkage coefficient itself, which could partially offset the claimed benefits especially in the very-low-rollout regime that the paper motivates as its target use case.

Statistical rigor of the main results is inconsistent: only the small-scale GSM8k/Qwen2.5-0.5B comparison (Table 2/5) uses multiple seeds (5) with reported variability; the larger-scale math, logic-puzzle, multimodal, and RLHF experiments (Figures 2-6, Table 1) appear to be single runs without error bars or significance testing, making it harder to rule out run-to-run noise as an explanation for some of the reported gains.

No direct empirical comparison against actor-critic (learned value-function) baselines is provided, despite this being a natural comparison point given the paper's framing around avoiding the cost of learned critics; the comparison is entirely among critic-free baselines.

The impact statement is essentially a boilerplate non-statement, and limitations of the approach (e.g., behavior under extreme reward sparsity/degenerate variance, sensitivity to batch composition, non-stationarity of v2/s2 estimates as the policy changes rapidly) are not explicitly discussed in a dedicated limitations section.

strengths: Clean and rigorous theoretical development: the paper carefully derives a bias-variance decomposition for baseline MSE (Eq. 4-6), motivates the James-Stein-style shrinkage baseline, and proves a closed-form optimal shrinkage coefficient (Theorem 1) using a leave-one-out construction that provably preserves unbiasedness of the policy gradient (Proposition 1). The proofs in the appendix are complete and correct as far as I can verify.

The method is genuinely practical: it requires no additional hyperparameters, adds negligible computational overhead (a few lines of code, shown in Listing 1), and is a true drop-in replacement for RLOO/GRPO-style baselines, which lowers the barrier to adoption.

Very extensive empirical validation spanning multiple model families and sizes (Qwen2.5-Math 1.5B/7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-Instruct 0.5B/1.5B/7B, Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B, Ministral-8B, Llama-3.2-3B), multiple task domains (math reasoning, logic puzzles, multimodal reasoning, RLHF with a Bradley-Terry reward model), and multiple competing baselines (GRPO, RLOO, ReMax, REINFORCE++, BLOO), consistently showing improvements.

The paper goes beyond simply reporting downstream accuracy: Appendix B directly verifies the theoretical claims by (1) comparing baseline MSE against a Monte-Carlo-estimated ground-truth value function, and (2) computing the L2 distance between estimated and ground-truth policy gradients using large-sample MC estimates. This is a rigorous and convincing way to substantiate the core variance-reduction claim rather than relying solely on end-task metrics.

Thoughtful ablations on adaptive shrinkage behavior (Figure 7, Appendix C) show the mechanism behaves sensibly with rollout count, training progress, dataset difficulty heterogeneity, and semantic heterogeneity, adding confidence that the method is robust rather than a lucky empirical fit.

The authors are appropriately careful/honest about the limits of the analogy to classical Stein estimation (non-Gaussian rewards, no formal minimax risk guarantee), which is a positive sign of scientific honesty rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: The theoretical optimality is derived for a relaxed surrogate objective (minimizing baseline MSE w.r.t. the value function, Eq. 3-5) rather than the true policy-gradient variance, which also depends on the score-function norm (acknowledged in Sec 3.1 as a 'standard simplification'). While Appendix B.2 partially validates the reduction in actual gradient L2 error, the core theorem's guarantee is only about the proxy objective, so the paper's language of 'provable variance reduction' for the policy gradient itself is slightly stronger than what is directly established.

Most of the main reported curves (Figures 2-6) appear to be based on a single training run per configuration, without seeds/confidence intervals, despite claims of consistent, non-trivial percentage gains (2.3%-15.2%); only the smaller-scale GSM8k ablation (Table 2/5) uses 5 seeds. This makes it hard to assess whether the reported improvements on the larger reasoning/multimodal/RLHF experiments are statistically robust versus run-to-run noise.

The plug-in estimates of v and s (Eqs. 13-14) used to compute λ̂ are themselves noisy, especially with small n or m typical of RLVR; the paper does not analyze how estimation error in λ̂ propagates into the bias/variance of the resulting gradient estimator beyond empirical demonstration, which would strengthen the theoretical completeness.

The conceptual contribution — applying a shrinkage/control-variate combination of local and global mean estimators — is a fairly natural extension of well-known bias-variance/control-variate ideas in classical statistics and RL; the technical novelty lies mainly in the specific leave-one-out unbiasedness construction and its application context to RLVR, rather than fundamentally new methodology.

No hyperparameter sensitivity or fairness checks (e.g., learning-rate sweeps for baselines) are reported to confirm that comparison partners (RLOO, GRPO, REINFORCE++, ReMax) were not under-tuned relative to the proposed method, which is a common concern in baseline comparison studies.
